title: The King Crowned with Thorns and Lifted Up
summary: Pilate has Jesus flogged and mocked, presents him to the crowd, and, pressed by the charge that releasing him would make Pilate no friend of Caesar, hands him over to be crucified. Jesus carries his cross to Golgotha, entrusts his mother to the beloved disciple, and dies saying “It is finished.” A soldier pierces his side, and Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus bury him in a new tomb in a garden.
story:
Chapter 18 ended with the crowd choosing Barabbas. Now the trial before Pilate reaches its verdict, and the hour Jesus has spoken of since Cana (2:4) arrives. Throughout the Gospel Jesus has said he would be lifted up and would draw all people to himself (3:14, 8:28, 12:32), and here the lifting up happens on a Roman cross. John tells the crucifixion with fewer details of agony than the other Gospels and more attention to meaning: Scripture fulfilled at each step, Jesus in command of his own death, his kingship announced over the cross in three languages, and his last word a cry of completion.

The chapter gathers threads from the whole book. Jesus dies on the day of Preparation as the Passover lambs are being made ready, recalling John the Baptist's first cry, “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (1:29). His mother, last seen at Cana, reappears at the cross, and the word Woman and the theme of the hour return with her. Nicodemus, who came by night in chapter 3 and spoke up cautiously in 7:50-51, now comes openly with a king's portion of spices. The chapter ends in silence, with the body in a garden tomb as the Sabbath begins, and waits for the morning of chapter 20.
historical:
Crucifixion was Rome's most shameful punishment, used chiefly for slaves, rebels, and provincials without citizenship. Cicero, prosecuting a corrupt governor of Sicily in 70 BC, called it the cruelest and most disgusting penalty and said the very word cross should be kept far from a Roman citizen's body, eyes, and ears (Against Verres 2.5.165-169). Judea knew it well. The Hasmonean king Alexander Jannaeus crucified eight hundred of his Jewish opponents about 88 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 13.380), an act the Dead Sea Scrolls remember with horror as hanging men alive (4Q169, the Nahum commentary); the Syrian legate Varus crucified two thousand rebels after Herod's death in 4 BC (Antiquities 17.295); and during the siege of AD 70 Titus crucified as many as five hundred captives a day (Jewish War 5.449-451). It was public by design, meant to terrify.

Flogging usually came first, with a whip of leather thongs that could be weighted with bone or metal, and it alone could kill. John places the flogging in the middle of the trial (verse 1), perhaps as Pilate's attempt to satisfy the crowd without an execution, while Mark places it with the sentence (Mark 15:15). The condemned carried the crossbeam to the place of execution, where he was tied or nailed to it and raised on an upright post; John says Jesus carried his own cross and does not mention Simon of Cyrene (Mark 15:21). Physical evidence is rare, because nails were usually removed and reused. In 1968 an ossuary found at Giv'at ha-Mivtar in north Jerusalem held the bones of a man named Yehohanan with an iron nail still through his heel bone. A reexamination by Joseph Zias and Eliezer Sekeles (1985) concluded that his arms were probably tied rather than nailed and questioned the earlier claim that his legs had been broken. His burial in a family tomb shows that a crucified man in Jerusalem could receive Jewish burial. Death came slowly, often through exhaustion, shock, and difficulty breathing, which is why breaking the legs (the crurifragium) hastened it.

The notice fastened to the cross, the titulus, announced the charge. Suetonius describes a condemned slave led through a banquet with a placard stating his crime (Caligula 32), and the letter of the churches of Lyons and Vienne tells of the martyr Attalus led around the amphitheater in AD 177 behind a tablet reading, in Latin, that he was a Christian (Eusebius, Church History 5.1.44). Pilate's was written in Hebrew (probably meaning Aramaic, the spoken language of Judea), Latin, the language of Roman law, and Greek, the common tongue of the eastern empire.

Golgotha lay outside the city wall but near it and near a road. Since the fourth century it has been located at the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, built by the emperor Constantine and dedicated in 335 (Eusebius, Life of Constantine 3.25-40); excavations show the site was an old quarry outside the wall of Jesus' day, with rock-cut tombs of the first century nearby. The Garden Tomb north of the Damascus Gate, proposed by General Charles Gordon in 1883, is a place of prayer for many, but Gabriel Barkay has shown that its tomb was cut in the Iron Age, centuries before Jesus.

The cry that releasing Jesus would make Pilate no friend of Caesar (verse 12) touched a real fear. Friend of Caesar (amicus Caesaris) could be an honorific for trusted men, and under Tiberius charges of treason (maiestas) were frequent and deadly, as Tacitus's account of the reign shows. Paul Maier (Church History, 1968) suggested that if the crucifixion took place after the fall of Pilate's possible patron Sejanus in October AD 31, Pilate would have been especially exposed; the link is a hypothesis, not a fact. The timing within the day matters to John. He says it was the day of Preparation for the Passover, about the sixth hour (verse 14), that is, about noon on the day before the Passover meal. In Jewish usage the Preparation was the day before the Sabbath, Friday (Mark 15:42; compare Josephus, Antiquities 16.163 and Didache 8:1), and the Passover lambs were slaughtered in the temple that afternoon, between the ninth and eleventh hours (Jewish War 6.423).
cultural:
The soldiers' mockery parodies a royal investiture. The crown of thorns mimics the wreath of a victor or ruler, the purple robe (purple dye was costly and associated with kings; Mark calls it purple, Matthew a scarlet military cloak) stands in for royal dress, and the greeting “Hail, King of the Jews!” echoes the salute given to Caesar. The slaps (verse 3) turn homage into contempt. Pilate's “Here is the man!” (verse 5) may be pity, contempt, or an attempt to show that this broken figure is no threat. The charge that Jesus had declared himself the Son of God (verse 7) rests on the law against blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16), and for Pilate the phrase would carry other overtones: Augustus had called himself son of the deified Julius, and Greco-Roman stories told of divine men. That may be why he becomes more afraid and asks, “Where are You from?” (verses 8 and 9), a question John's readers know is the deepest one about Jesus (7:27-29, 8:14).

The judgment seat (bēma) was the raised platform from which a Roman magistrate gave formal sentence. John names the place in Greek, Lithostrotos, the Stone Pavement, and in Aramaic, Gabbatha; the two names are not translations of each other, and the Aramaic is usually thought to mean a height or ridge.

The clothes of the condemned went to the execution squad, here four soldiers. The tunic (chitōn), the garment worn next to the skin, was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom. Josephus says the high priest's robe was woven as a single garment rather than made of two pieces sewn at the shoulders and sides (Antiquities 3.161), and some interpreters see a hint of Christ's priesthood here, though John does not say so. The women standing near the cross were in a place of danger and devotion; mourning for the crucified could be treated as sympathy with a criminal. John names Jesus' mother, her sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. Whether that is three or four women is debated; the second-century writer Hegesippus says Clopas was the brother of Joseph (Eusebius, Church History 3.11). A dying son's provision for his widowed mother was a duty of honor, and Jesus fulfills it from the cross.

The sour wine (oxos) was the cheap wine vinegar soldiers drank, posca in Latin, and a jar of it was at hand. Hyssop, a small bushy plant, was used to sprinkle the blood of the first Passover on the doorposts (Exodus 12:22) and in rites of cleansing (Psalm 51:7). Jewish law required that the body of an executed man not remain on a tree overnight (Deuteronomy 21:22-23), and Josephus says the Jews took down the crucified and buried them before sunset (Jewish War 4.317). The concern was sharper because the next day was a Sabbath that coincided with the first day of the festival, which John calls a High Sabbath.

Jewish burial did not embalm the body as the Egyptians did. The body was washed and anointed (the Mishnah allows this even on the Sabbath, m. Shabbat 23:5), wrapped in linen with spices to honor the dead and mask decay, and laid in a tomb, often a chamber cut into rock. Executed criminals were normally buried apart, not in family tombs (m. Sanhedrin 6:5), which makes Joseph's gift of a new tomb all the more striking. Nicodemus brings about a hundred Roman pounds (litrai, roughly 33 kilograms or 75 pounds) of myrrh and aloes. Josephus describes five hundred servants carrying spices at Herod the Great's funeral (Antiquities 17.199); Nicodemus gives Jesus a burial fit for a king. Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council according to Mark 15:43, and Nicodemus, the Pharisee who first came to Jesus at night (3:1-2), both step into the open at the moment when association with Jesus is most costly.
literary:
The chapter completes the seven scenes of the Roman trial that began in 18:28. Pilate brings Jesus out twice with a presentation formula: “Here is the man!” (verse 5) and “Here is your King!” (verse 14). Between them the charge shifts from politics to theology (verse 7) and back to politics (verse 12). At verse 13 Pilate sits on the judgment seat, but the Greek verb (ekathisen) can also be read transitively, that Pilate seated Jesus on the judgment seat. The second-century Gospel of Peter (3.7) and Justin Martyr (First Apology 35) both tell the mockery that way, with Jesus set on the seat and told to judge; most modern translations read it intransitively, but some interpreters think John intends the double meaning: the prisoner is the true judge. The trial ends with the chief priests' declaration, “We have no king but Caesar” (verse 15), a denial of the confession of God as Israel's king (Judges 8:23, 1 Samuel 8:7).

At the cross John arranges a series of short scenes, each marked by fulfillment or testimony: the title (verses 19 to 22), the garments (23 and 24), the mother and the disciple (25 to 27), the thirst and the last word (28 to 30), the pierced side (31 to 37), and the burial (38 to 42). Raymond Brown and others have noted the careful balance of these episodes. Four times John says Scripture was fulfilled (verses 24, 28, 36, and 37), a denser cluster than anywhere else in the Gospel. Jesus' last word, tetelestai, “It is finished,” picks up the Gospel's language of completing the Father's work (4:34, 5:36, 17:4) and of loving his own to the end, eis telos (13:1). John does not say Jesus breathed his last, as Mark does, but that he bowed his head and handed over (paredōken) his spirit, the same verb used throughout the passion for others handing him over.

In verse 35 the narrator steps out of the story with an eyewitness claim, one of the clearest statements of purpose in the Gospel, echoed at 20:31 and 21:24. The passion is also framed by gardens: it begins in a garden across the Kidron (18:1) and ends in a garden with a new tomb (19:41), and in the next chapter Mary will mistake the risen Jesus for the gardener. Many readers hear an echo of Eden, though John does not make it explicit.

outline.t: Flogged, mocked, and presented: Here is the man
Pilate afraid: authority given from above
The judgment seat: We have no king but Caesar
Crucified at Golgotha under the title King of the Jews
Jesus gives his mother to the beloved disciple
I am thirsty; It is finished
The pierced side and the Scripture fulfilled
Burial by Joseph and Nicodemus in a new tomb

doctrines.note: Jesus is sentenced about noon on the day of Preparation for the Passover and dies as the lambs are being slaughtered in the temple. John applies to him the Passover rule that none of the lamb's bones may be broken (verse 36; Exodus 12:46, Numbers 9:12; compare Psalm 34:20), and hyssop, used to apply the blood of the first Passover (Exodus 12:22), lifts the wine to his lips. The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (1:29) finishes the work the Father gave him (verse 30).

Four times John says Scripture was fulfilled: the dividing of the garments (Psalm 22:18), the thirst (Psalm 69:21), the unbroken bones (Exodus 12:46, Psalm 34:20), and the pierced one (Zechariah 12:10). Some are psalms of the righteous sufferer, read as patterns completed in Jesus; Zechariah is a prophecy of mourning and cleansing (Zechariah 12:10-13:1). John presents the whole event as the story Scripture was already telling.

The chapter is about kingship. Jesus is crowned, robed, hailed, presented as “your King,” and enthroned on a cross under a title Pilate refuses to change. The priests' “We have no king but Caesar” shows what is at stake. The seamless tunic may hint at Christ's priesthood, and his giving of his own life fulfills the priestly work of offering; John leaves the priestly echo implicit and makes the kingship explicit.

In John the cross is not a humiliation later reversed by glory; it is the hour of glory (12:23, 17:1). The Son of Man is lifted up (3:14, 12:32) on the cross itself, and the one who has glorified the Father by accomplishing his work (17:4) completes it there. The glory is seen through the shame, not in spite of it.

Pilate claims authority to release or to crucify (verse 10), and Jesus answers that he would have none unless it were given from above (verse 11). The state's power is real and borrowed; it answers to God, and those who use it are accountable. Jesus also distinguishes degrees of guilt: the one who handed him over bears the greater sin, but Pilate's is not thereby excused.

words.note: Teleō, to finish, complete, carry out, fulfill. It occurs about 28 times in the New Testament and in John only in verses 28 and 30. Jesus' last word is a single Greek verb in the perfect tense, tetelestai, “It is finished”: the work the Father gave him (17:4) is complete and its result stands. It is a cry of accomplishment, not of defeat. The related verb teleioō is used just before it for Scripture being fulfilled (verse 28). Popular preaching sometimes says tetelestai was the stamp on a paid receipt; the verb was used in commercial papyri for paying taxes and debts, but it is a general word for completing anything, and the sense here comes from John's own language of finishing the Father's work.

Stauroō, to crucify, occurs about 46 times in the New Testament and 11 times in this chapter, first as the crowd's demand (verses 6 and 15) and then as the soldiers' act (verses 18, 20, 23). The noun stauros originally meant an upright stake. In John's Gospel crucifixion is also the lifting up of the Son of Man (3:14, 12:32-33), so the most degrading form of death becomes the place where Jesus is exalted. Paul can say he resolved to know nothing but Christ crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2), turning the word of shame into the center of the message.

Ekkenteō, to pierce, stab through, occurs in the New Testament only in verse 37 and Revelation 1:7, both drawing on Zechariah 12:10. The Hebrew of Zechariah says the people will look on the one they pierced and mourn for him as for an only son. The older Greek translation (the Septuagint) has a different verb, that they danced insultingly or mocked, apparently from a different reading of the Hebrew; the later Greek versions of Aquila and Theodotion have exekentēsan, they pierced. John's wording agrees with the Hebrew and those later versions, not with the Septuagint.

Paraskeuē, preparation, occurs six times in the New Testament, always of the day before a Sabbath or feast (Matthew 27:62, Mark 15:42, Luke 23:54, and three times in this chapter). In Jewish Greek it had become the ordinary name for Friday, the day on which food was prepared for the Sabbath, and it is still the word for Friday in modern Greek. The phrase “the day of Preparation for the Passover” (verse 14) can mean the day before the Passover meal or the Friday of Passover week; how to read it is at the center of the debate over John's chronology.

Exousia, authority, right, power to act, occurs about 102 times in the New Testament. BDAG distinguishes the right to act from the capacity to act, and both are at stake here. Pilate claims exousia to release or crucify (verse 10); Jesus replies that Pilate would have none over him unless it were given from above (verse 11). Earlier Jesus said that he himself has exousia to lay down his life and to take it up again (10:18). Pilate's authority is delegated; the Son's is his own, and he uses it to die.

Anōthen, from above, from the top, or again, anew. It occurs 13 times in the New Testament. In 3:3 and 3:7 its double meaning drives the Nicodemus conversation: to be born from above or born again. In this chapter it appears twice with two senses: Pilate's authority is given from above (verse 11), and the tunic is woven from the top (verse 23). The first reminds the reader that heaven, not Rome, holds final authority.

Chitōn, tunic, the long garment worn next to the skin under the outer cloak (himation), occurs 11 times in the New Testament. John notes that Jesus' tunic was seamless, woven in one piece, which is why the soldiers cast lots for it rather than tearing it. The detail fulfills the parallel lines of Psalm 22:18, garments divided and clothing allotted. Because the high priest's robe was woven in one piece (Josephus, Antiquities 3.161), some see a priestly allusion, and Cyprian (On the Unity of the Church 7, about 251) made the untorn tunic a picture of the church's unity; neither reading is stated by John.

Paradidōmi, to hand over, deliver up. It occurs about 120 times in the New Testament and runs through John's passion: Judas hands Jesus over, the priests hand him to Pilate, and Pilate hands him over to be crucified (verse 16). In verse 30 the same verb describes Jesus' own act: he bowed his head and handed over his spirit. BDAG lists the sense of giving up one's spirit, and John's choice of this verb, rather than the Synoptic exepneusen, he breathed his last, makes Jesus the agent of his own death, as he said he would be (10:18).

christ:
Everything in John has pointed here. Jesus is the King enthroned on a cross, proclaimed in the three languages of the world, and the chief priests' attempt to edit the title only fixes it: “What I have written, I have written” (verse 22). He is the Lamb whose bones are not broken, dying on the day of Preparation, and the true Passover of which Paul says “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). He is the righteous sufferer of the Psalms, whose garments are divided (Psalm 22) and who is given sour wine for his thirst (Psalm 69). He is the pierced one of Zechariah 12:10, on whom Israel will look with mourning, and in the next verse of that prophecy a fountain is opened to cleanse from sin (Zechariah 13:1).

He is in command to the end. He knows that everything has been accomplished, speaks so that Scripture is fulfilled, and hands over his spirit rather than having it taken (10:18). His concern for his mother in his last hour shows his humanity as clearly as his words show his authority, and in giving the beloved disciple to her and her to him he forms the first household of the new family he came to create, those born of God (1:12-13).

The flow of blood and water from his side has been read in several ways, and the readings are not exclusive. It proves that he truly died, against any teaching that he only seemed to suffer (compare 1 John 5:6). It points to the life and cleansing that flow from his death, fulfilling his promise that streams of living water would flow from within (7:37-39) and recalling the river from the temple in Ezekiel 47. And many in the church, from the fathers onward, have seen in the water and the blood baptism and the Lord's Supper, which flow from the cross. John's own stated purpose is simpler: the eyewitness testifies “so that you also may believe” (verse 35). The Son of God truly died, which is the necessary ground of the resurrection that follows, and he was buried with honor by two men who had been afraid to follow him openly until the moment it cost the most.
interpretation:
The earliest Christian sermon on the Passover that survives outside the New Testament, Melito of Sardis's Peri Pascha (about 160 to 170), reads the passion through the Exodus lamb with great beauty and also contains the first known explicit charge that Israel murdered God, a charge that shadowed Christian preaching for centuries. Jewish tradition preserved a different memory in the Babylonian Talmud, which dates the execution of Yeshu to the eve of Passover (b. Sanhedrin 43a), the same day John gives.

The fathers found the church's sacraments in the pierced side. Augustine, whose Latin Bible said the soldier opened rather than pierced the side, called it the opening of the door of life from which the sacraments flowed (Tractates on John 120). John Chrysostom, in his third baptismal instruction, taught that the water signified baptism and the blood the Eucharist, and that as Eve was formed from the side of the sleeping Adam, so the church was formed from the side of Christ. Cyprian made the seamless tunic a figure of the church's unity (On the Unity of the Church 7). Augustine also read the entrusting of Mary to the beloved disciple as Jesus teaching by example the duty of children to their parents (Tractate 119). The apocryphal Gospel of Nicodemus, in its later forms, named the soldier with the spear Longinus, and a legend of his conversion grew around the name.

Medieval devotion lingered at the cross. The thirteenth-century hymn Stabat Mater, attributed to Jacopone da Todi among others, takes its opening from verse 25, Mary standing by the cross, and was later set by composers from Josquin to Pergolesi. Devotion to the wounds of Christ and, later, to the Sacred Heart drew on verse 34. Matthias Grünewald's Isenheim Altarpiece (1512 to 1516, now in Colmar) sets John the Baptist beside the crucified Christ, pointing to him, with a lamb at his feet whose blood flows into a chalice, a painted commentary on John 1:29 and 19:36.

The Reformers read tetelestai as the finished sacrifice. Calvin's commentary (1553) presses the point that nothing is left to be added to Christ's offering, a reading that became central in Protestant objections to the sacrifice of the Mass. Catholic teaching, for its part, found in verses 26 and 27 Mary's motherhood of the church: the Second Vatican Council's Lumen Gentium (1964, section 58) says that the dying Christ gave her as mother to his disciple. Protestant interpreters have generally read the scene as filial care and the forming of the new family of disciples.

In liturgy, John's passion is the Gospel for Good Friday across much of the church. Three of the traditional Seven Last Words come from this chapter (Woman, here is your son; I am thirsty; It is finished), and Joseph Haydn's The Seven Last Words of Our Saviour on the Cross (1787) was written for a Good Friday meditation in Cádiz. In Bach's St John Passion (1724) the alto aria on It is finished stands at the emotional center of the work. Modern study, from C. H. Dodd's Historical Tradition in the Fourth Gospel (1963) to Raymond Brown's The Death of the Messiah (1994), has argued that John preserves independent and sometimes early tradition about the day and the details of the crucifixion, even while shaping them theologically.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles come from the Greek manuscripts. In verse 3 the words ‘they went up to Him again and again’ are absent from the Byzantine manuscripts behind the King James Version, which reads only ‘And said, Hail, King of the Jews’. In verse 14 a few manuscripts, among them Codex Regius (L), Codex Delta, and a later corrector of Sinaiticus, read ‘about the third hour’, which would agree with Mark 15:25; an ancient explanation, later associated with Eusebius, suggested that a scribe had confused the Greek numeral letters for three and six. The great majority of manuscripts and all modern editions read the sixth hour. In verse 20 the King James Version lists the languages as ‘Hebrew, and Greek, and Latin’, following the Byzantine order; the earliest manuscripts have Hebrew, Latin, and Greek.

In verse 29 every manuscript except one or two late minuscules reads hyssōpō, on hyssop. In the sixteenth century Joachim Camerarius conjectured hyssō, on a javelin, the Roman soldier's pilum, which would be easier to picture; minuscule 476 happens to read that, probably by accident. Modern editions keep hyssop, which fits John's Passover imagery. In verse 35 the manuscripts divide, as at 20:31, between a present and an aorist form of believe, that is, that you may keep believing or that you may come to believe. In verse 39 Codex Sinaiticus in its first hand and Codex Vaticanus read heligma, a roll or package, instead of migma, a mixture; modern editions print mixture.

A related variant appears in another Gospel. In Matthew 27:49 Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and several other manuscripts add that another took a spear and pierced his side, and water and blood came out, placing the piercing before Jesus' death. Most textual critics judge this an early insertion from John 19:34, perhaps through a harmony of the Gospels, and modern English versions leave it out of Matthew or put it in a note.

Translation differences are also visible. In verse 13 Gabbatha is said to be ‘in the Hebrew’ (KJV, BSB) or ‘in Aramaic’ (NIV); the word is Aramaic, which John, like other Greek writers, calls Hebrew. In verse 30 the BSB's ‘yielded up His spirit’, the ESV's ‘gave up his spirit’, and the KJV's ‘gave up the ghost’ render the same verb. In verse 40 the othonia are ‘linen clothes’ (KJV), ‘linen cloths’ (ESV, BSB), or ‘strips of linen’ (NIV).

teach.big: On the cross Jesus is revealed as the true King and the Passover Lamb, who freely completes the work the Father gave him and whose death, witnessed and recorded, calls for faith.

outline.t: The world's mockery of kingship becomes, unknowingly, the truth: this beaten man is the King, and Pilate's ‘Here is the man’ presents humanity at its most wounded.
Earthly power is real but borrowed; Pilate's authority comes from above, and fear of losing status drives his choices.
The chief priests' cry, ‘We have no king but Caesar’, shows what rejecting Jesus finally means: choosing a lesser king.
Jesus carries his own cross, and the title over it proclaims to the whole world what his enemies meant as mockery.
Even the soldiers' gambling fulfills Scripture: nothing in the passion is outside God's purpose.
In his agony Jesus cares for his mother and forms a new family of disciples who belong to one another.
“It is finished” is a cry of completion: the Father's work is done and nothing needs to be added.
The witness insists that Jesus truly died, and the blood and water point to the life that flows from his death.
Secret disciples become public at the costliest moment; honoring Jesus when all seems lost is an act of faith.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first is to preach the cross chiefly as a catalog of physical suffering. John tells it with restraint; his emphasis is on meaning, fulfillment, and Jesus' sovereign freedom, and a sermon that dwells on medical detail can miss what John is saying. A second is to repeat claims as facts that the text and evidence do not support: that tetelestai was a technical word stamped on receipts, that blood and water prove a specific medical condition, or that the Garden Tomb is the site of the burial.

A third, and the most serious, is to blame the Jews collectively. The chief priests' cry in verse 15 is the act of particular leaders in a particular crisis, and the crowd, the soldiers, Pilate, and the absent disciples all play their part. The church's own teaching places every sinner at the cross. A fourth is to force the chronology debate into a crisis of faith or to dismiss it; it is a real question, discussed below, on which faithful scholars differ. A fifth is to use verses 26 and 27 as a battleground only. Catholic and Orthodox teaching finds here Mary's spiritual motherhood; Protestant readers emphasize Jesus' filial care and the new community of disciples. Teachers can name both while keeping the scene's plain force, a dying son providing for his mother and binding his followers into one household.
teach.pastoral: This chapter presses on people who have watched someone they love die, especially slowly or unjustly. Mary standing at the cross gives them a companion in the text, and Jesus' care for her in his own agony tells them that grief and love are not forgotten by God. It presses on those who have been humiliated, stripped, or mocked, including survivors of abuse; Jesus endured public shame, and teachers should say so with care and without making anyone relive their own story in public. It presses on those whose faith has been secret, like Joseph and Nicodemus. And it presses on those who fear that their sin is too great, who need to hear plainly what It is finished means.

hard.q: Did Jesus die on the day of Passover or the day before, and why does John seem to differ from the other Gospels?
hard.a:
The objection is clear and strong. Matthew, Mark, and Luke present the Last Supper as a Passover meal, prepared on the first day of Unleavened Bread when the Passover lamb was sacrificed (Mark 14:12-16), which puts the crucifixion on the next day, the fifteenth of Nisan, the feast day itself. John says the leaders had not yet eaten the Passover when they brought Jesus to Pilate (18:28), that Pilate's sentence came on the day of Preparation for the Passover about the sixth hour (19:14), and that the following Sabbath was a High Sabbath (19:31), all of which puts the crucifixion on the fourteenth, when the lambs were slaughtered. Mark also says Jesus was crucified at the third hour (Mark 15:25), while in John the sentence is still being given about the sixth. Bart Ehrman (Jesus, Interrupted, 2009, and elsewhere) is among many scholars who argue that John or his source moved the day and hour to make a theological point: Jesus dies as the Passover lamb.

There are three main responses, each held by careful scholars. The first agrees that the accounts differ but judges John's date to be the historical one. John P. Meier (A Marginal Jew, volume 1, 1991) and Raymond Brown (The Death of the Messiah, 1994) favored the Johannine chronology, noting that a trial and execution on the feast day itself would be surprising, that the Talmud also dates the execution to the eve of Passover (b. Sanhedrin 43a), and that the Synoptic meal may have been a farewell meal with Passover features. Pope Benedict XVI (Jesus of Nazareth: Holy Week, 2011) followed this view. Astronomical calculations fit it well: the fourteenth of Nisan fell on a Friday in both AD 30 and AD 33 (Humphreys and Waddington, 1983).

The second holds that the accounts can be harmonized in favor of the Synoptic date. On this reading, to eat the Passover in 18:28 can refer to the festival meals of the whole seven-day feast, including the sacrifice called the chagigah, and the Preparation of the Passover in 19:14 means the Friday of Passover week, since paraskeuē was the ordinary word for Friday. D. A. Carson (The Gospel According to John, 1991) and Craig Blomberg (The Historical Reliability of John's Gospel, 2001) have argued this way, following older scholars such as Theodor Zahn.

The third proposes that different calendars were in use. Annie Jaubert (La date de la Cène, 1957) argued that Jesus followed the solar calendar known from Qumran and ate the Passover on Tuesday evening; Colin Humphreys (The Mystery of the Last Supper, 2011) argued for an older lunar reckoning that put the meal on Wednesday. Both explain why the Synoptics call the meal a Passover while John dates the official Passover later; critics reply that there is no evidence Jesus used a sectarian calendar or that the temple would have slaughtered lambs for such a Passover.

On the hour, some older writers proposed that John counted from midnight in a Roman fashion, but most now think both Gospels use broad blocks of the day (the third hour for mid-morning, the sixth for midday) and that neither was measuring with a clock; a few manuscripts even read third in John. All four Gospels agree on what matters most: Jesus died on a Friday at Passover time, under Pontius Pilate, and rose on the first day of the week. Whether John has adjusted the date for theological reasons, preserved the more accurate date, or used language that fits the Synoptic date is a second-order question on which faithful readers disagree.

hard.q: Was Jesus really buried in a tomb, or is the burial story a later legend?
hard.a:
The skeptical case begins with Roman practice. Crucified bodies were often left on the cross for days as a warning and then thrown into common graves or left to animals. John Dominic Crossan (Jesus: A Revolutionary Biography, 1994) argued that Jesus' body was probably dealt with in this way and that the story of an honorable burial by Joseph of Arimathea arose later, perhaps to answer that shame. Bart Ehrman (How Jesus Became God, 2014) came to a similar conclusion, judging it unlikely that Pilate would release the body of a man executed as a would-be king, and holding that if there was no known tomb, the empty tomb stories are later too.

Others answer that the Jewish setting changes the picture. Deuteronomy 21:22-23 required burial before nightfall, and Josephus says that Jews took down even the crucified and buried them before sunset (Jewish War 4.317). The ossuary of Yehohanan shows that at least one crucified man in first-century Jerusalem was placed in a family tomb, and Craig Evans has argued from this and from Jewish burial law that Roman governors in peacetime generally allowed Jewish burial of the executed. Joseph of Arimathea is an unlikely invention: he is a member of the council that condemned Jesus (Mark 15:43), named, and tied to a real place, and the tradition of his burial of Jesus appears in all four Gospels and is presupposed in Paul's early summary that Christ died, was buried, and was raised (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Raymond Brown (The Death of the Messiah, 1994) judged the burial by Joseph to be very probably historical. Readers who do not share Christian faith may still weigh these arguments differently, and the debate often turns on how much weight is given to the Gospels' specific testimony against general Roman practice.

observe: What three titles or presentations does Pilate use for Jesus in verses 5, 14, and 19, and how do the chief priests respond to each?
Which four passages of Scripture does John say were fulfilled in this chapter, and what event is linked to each?
Who comes to bury Jesus, what do they bring, and where do they lay him?
interpret: Why do you think John records Jesus' last word as “It is finished” rather than a cry of anguish? What has been finished?
What does Jesus mean when he tells Pilate that his authority is given from above, and how does that change the way the scene should be read?
Why might John emphasize that Jesus died on the day of Preparation and that none of his bones were broken?
apply: Joseph and Nicodemus had been secret disciples. What would it cost you to identify openly with Jesus in the places where you live and work?
Jesus provided for his mother while dying. What does his example say about responsibility for family and for the family of believers?
If the work is truly finished, what are you still trying to add to it in order to feel accepted by God?
